passage: Noor, you asked why my kitchen has two tiffin boxes. Let your old Hansa Ba tell you. When I was twenty-four and newly running my own house in Ahmedabad, we were strict Jain: no onion, no garlic, nothing after sunset. My husband's colleague, Mr. Fernandes, was coming to dinner with his wife, and I panicked. Would they find our food bland? My mother-in-law said, 'Serve what we eat, and they'll learn.' Instead I cooked our dal as always, bought a small tin of fried onions from the market, set it on a separate plate at their places, and said, 'Please, as you like.' Mrs. Fernandes cried, 'You thought of us!' We ate together for forty years after that. My food stayed mine. My table became everyone's.

qa.q: Where was Hansa running her own house at twenty-four?
qa.a: In Ahmedabad.

qa.q: What was young Hansa feeling before the Fernandes dinner?
qa.a: She felt panicked and anxious that the guests would find her Jain food bland.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the dinner work, and why?
qa.a: Hansa kept her own dal but set fried onions on a separate plate for the guests, so she honoured her custom and still gave them a choice.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Fernandes experience Hansa's gesture?
qa.a: She felt touched and cared for, crying, 'You thought of us!', which began a forty-year friendship.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps her family's food custom at home yet offers guests a choice and never mocks their plate, so tradition does not become a wall.

passage: Saga Dawa month meant no meat in Tenzin's kitchen, the way it had been in Ama's house in Dharamshala. But tonight six friends were coming, Simran among them, the one who called any meal without chicken 'just a snack'. Then the rain knocked out the power, leaving one gas burner and a torch. Tenzin, twenty-five, made a big pot of vegetable thenthuk and, with the last of the phone battery, ordered a plate of chicken momos from the corner shop for anyone who wanted them, kept on a separate plate by the door. Simran arrived dripping, laughed at the torchlight, then went back for the thenthuk twice. 'Okay, this is not a snack.' Nobody teased anyone's plate. The momos disappeared too.

qa.q: What did Tenzin cook in the big pot?
qa.a: Vegetable thenthuk.

qa.q: What was Tenzin probably feeling when the power went out with six friends on the way?
qa.a: Tenzin was probably worried and under pressure, with one burner, a torch and guests coming, yet calm enough to plan.

qa.q: How did Tenzin keep the custom and still welcome everyone, despite the power cut?
qa.a: Tenzin kept the kitchen meat-free but offered chicken momos from outside on a separate plate, and nobody mocked anyone's choice.

qa.q: How did Simran's view of a meatless meal change?
qa.a: Simran moved from calling it 'just a snack' to going back twice and saying so, because it was offered warmly, without a lecture.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who keeps a family food custom at home while offering guests a choice and never mocking anyone's plate.

passage:
At her housewarming in the new Chennai flat, Gopika had cooked the way her grandmother did: a full vegetarian meal, sambar, three poriyals, payasam. Her kitchen would stay vegetarian; that part mattered to her.

Then Nitin arrived, beaming, with a large box. "Chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane!"

Two of her cousins exchanged a look.

Gopika hesitated only a second. "Thank you, Nitin, that's so kind." She set up a small table on the balcony with its own plates and serving spoon. "Biryani lovers, this way. Sambar lovers, that way. Both, both."

Everyone laughed. When a cousin muttered something about the smell in the house, Gopika said lightly, "Nobody's plate is up for comments today, Anna."

By evening the biryani box and the payasam pot were both empty.

qa.q: What did Nitin bring to the housewarming?
qa.a: Nitin brought chicken biryani from the best place in Triplicane.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling when Nitin arrived with the box?
qa.a: Gopika felt briefly torn between her vegetarian kitchen and not wanting Nitin to feel unwelcome, before choosing warmth.

qa.q: How did Gopika keep her tradition and still respect her guests?
qa.a: She kept her kitchen vegetarian but set up a separate balcony table for the biryani, thanked Nitin, and stopped her cousin's remark about the smell.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt when the cousins exchanged a look?
qa.a: Nitin might have felt awkward and unsure he had made a mistake, until Gopika's thanks and joke made him welcome.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps her family's vegetarian kitchen while offering guests a choice and allowing no mockery of anyone's plate.

passage:
"Your friend is coming tonight?" Hansa put down the ladle. "What will he eat? We don't cook onion, garlic, nothing."
"Ma, Aslam loves your dal-dhokli. He's eaten it from my tiffin a hundred times."
"But he eats meat at home."
"At home. Here he eats what we eat, and he asked me if there's anything he shouldn't bring. I told him to just bring himself."
Hansa wiped her hands slowly. "And the plates?"
Pradeep sat down next to her. "The same plates, Ma. He's my friend, not a problem to manage. Our kitchen stays our way; that's fair. But nobody gets a separate plate."
Hansa was quiet. Then: "Does he like it spicy?"
"Very."
"Then I'll add green chilli to his." She almost smiled. "Not to your father's."

qa.q: What dish does Aslam love?
qa.a: Aslam loves Ma's dal-dhokli.

qa.q: What was Hansa worried about when she asked about the plates?
qa.a: Hansa felt uneasy about purity, worried whether a meat-eating guest should use the family's plates.

qa.q: How does Pradeep balance the family custom and respect for Aslam?
qa.a: He keeps the kitchen's no-onion, no-garlic custom but refuses a separate plate, treating Aslam as a friend rather than a problem.

qa.q: How might Aslam feel if he knew about the plate talk?
qa.a: Aslam would likely feel relieved and respected that Pradeep insisted on the same plates, and welcomed as a friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps the family's food custom at home while refusing to let it become a wall against a guest.

passage:
I'm Amandeep, and this Gurpurab I took my colleague Dilnaz and her parents to the langar at our gurdwara in Pune.

I'd worried all week. They eat fish and meat at home; would the food seem plain? Would anyone stare?

At the langar everyone sits in rows on the floor, and the same dal, roti and kheer is served to everyone: a sweeper, a shop owner, Dilnaz's father. That is the whole point of it. Dilnaz's mother asked for seconds of the kheer.

Afterwards at home, Biji asked if she should make something special for them. I said, make what we make, and ask if they'd like anything else. Dilnaz's father asked for the saag recipe.

At their Navroz a month later, they put a full vegetarian plate in front of me without my asking, next to their sali boti. Nobody said a word about anybody's plate.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's mother ask for seconds of?
qa.a: Dilnaz's mother asked for seconds of the kheer.

qa.q: What was Amandeep worried about before taking Dilnaz's family to the langar?
qa.a: Amandeep felt anxious that they might find the food plain or feel stared at, since they eat fish and meat at home.

qa.q: How did Amandeep share the family's food tradition without making it a wall?
qa.a: By inviting them into the langar where everyone eats the same, asking Biji to cook as usual but offer anything else they'd like, and never commenting on plates.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz's family return the respect?
qa.a: At Navroz they served Amandeep a vegetarian plate without being asked, beside their own sali boti.

grounding: Shows a young adult who loves the family's food tradition, shares it openly with guests of another community, and never mocks anyone's plate.

passage:
Coordinator's note, Sunday community lunch, Lane 4 hall.
This month Asif volunteered to host. His family's kitchen is halal, and he cooked his Ammi's mutton korma the way she taught him. But he also made a big pot of dal, jeera rice and a paneer dish, and labelled each one clearly: "Veg", "Halal meat", "No onion-garlic" for the Jain family from Block C. He even asked Mrs Shah beforehand what spices she avoids.
When a teenager joked loudly about someone's "grass plate", Asif laughed but said, "Everyone's plate is good here," and served the boy extra dal. The boy had seconds.
At the end, old Mr Pillai, who is strictly vegetarian, told me he had never felt so welcome at a lunch run by "meat people". Asif heard, smiled, and said, "Next month you teach me your avial." I'd like Asif on the organising team.
Farida, coordinator

qa.q: What did Asif write on the labels?
qa.a: "Veg", "Halal meat" and "No onion-garlic".

qa.q: How might Asif have felt when the teenager joked about the grass plate?
qa.a: He was probably a little uncomfortable but calm, answering lightly that everyone's plate is good here.

qa.q: What did Asif do that balanced tradition and respect?
qa.a: He kept his family's halal cooking, offered clearly labelled choices for vegetarian and Jain guests, and never let anyone's food be mocked.

qa.q: How did Mr Pillai experience the lunch?
qa.a: Mr Pillai felt unusually welcome, enjoying food he could eat and a host who respected his vegetarian diet.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who keeps his family's food custom yet offers guests a choice and never mocks anyone's plate.
